titleStmt.title: Fixed Priority Timing Analysis of Real-Time Systems with Limited Parallelism

analytic.title: Fixed Priority Timing Analysis of Real-Time Systems with Limited Parallelism

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Conventional real-time system implementations assume a von Neumann processor-memory architecture with at most one software process executing at any time. Scheduling approaches for such systems multiplex the processor among runnable processes. Fixed priority scheduling, notably, utilises timing analysis to determine offline the run-time timing behaviour of the system. Recent alternative real-time system implementations combine processor-memory architectures with reconfigurable hardware for speedup. Such reconfigurable hardware can execute many functions in parallel. This leads to a limited parallel system where a single software process can execute on the processor at any time, in parallel with a number of functions implemented in hardware. Conventional fixed priority timing analysis is unsuitable for this model, as fundamental assumptions are compromised, eg. the notion of a critical instant. This paper proposes new timing analysis aimed at such limited parallel systems, illustrated by an example system utilising Field Programmable Gate Arrays as the reconfigurable hardware resource.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Architectures with processor and memory arranged on a single bus are typically assumed for real-time systems; at most one software process can then execute at any time; timing analysis models the multiplexing of the single processor among competing software processes. The analysis built up for such architectures is comprehensive, typified by the body of work based on fixed priority scheduling [11,9,10,3,4].

Recently developed real-time system implementations employ both reconfigurable hardware and a conventional processor, as target for the application functionality [7,16,17,18]. Thus, part of a software process is implemented in hardware so as to speed-up overall execution. The reconfigurable hardware can be seen as a number of application specific co-processors, where each one can speed-up the execution of the application (relative to a software implementation). Also, the co-processors can execute in parallel. In the resulting limited parallel architecture, at most one software process can execute in parallel with a number of co-processors.

Traditional co-processor use is exemplified by how floating point operations are achieved on a typical processor [12]: a running software process wishing to execute such an operation issues the latter to the floating point unit and the processor pauses until the floating point operation is complete. This typifies a master/slave approach to computation in co-processors, with the processor pausing whilst the co-processor executes, even if another runnable process could take advantage of the processor. An approach only viable if co-processor operations are short, wasting few cycles. The limited parallel model introduced here differs in that when a process is waiting for a hardware operation to complete, another runnable process can be scheduled.

Currently available reconfigurable devices support this model. Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) [15,19,1] can contain several million programmable gates: the Xilinx Virtex-II [19] FPGA can combine subsystems such as audio/image/signal processing, communications, networking etc. Such complex functions require many clock cycles to execute, thus the "master /slave" model becomes inefficient.

Reconfigurable logic can speed up overall system performance notably [6,7] and improve timing predictability [16,17,18] as no software scheduling is involved and the timing behaviour of logic is well-understood [19,15]. Timing analysis for conventional architectures is inappropriate for limited parallel systems. For example, the critical instant (worst-case scenario) forms the basis for all conventional fixed priority timing analysis -this worst-case no more applies under limited parallelism. Note that timing analyses developed for multiprocessor or distributed [13,8] systems are not applicable -both allow multiple software elements to execute in parallel on different processors and do not allow multiple application functions to execute in parallel on a single processor. This paper focuses on such limited parallel systems. It identifies a new worst-case scenario and provides suitable response-time analysis. It is structured as follows. In the next section, further background is given on the computational capabilities of systems involving reconfigurable hardware, providing motivation for the rest of the paper. In sections 3 and 4, timing analysis for limited parallel systems based on reconfigurable logic is given. In section 5, that analysis is assessed. Section 6 provides a case study: an implementation of a limited parallel system using FPGAs as the reconfigurable logic element. Section 7 provides concluding remarks.

div.head: Background/Motivation
div.p: We provide motivation for the limited parallel model, by reviewing architectures and implementations of actual embedded real-time systems. These are typically von Neumann processor-memory hierarchies (Figure 1 This model is supported by a wide range of technologies. Firstly, hybrid processors which contain processor and reconfigurable logic on the same device. Figure 2(a) shows a typical device, the Triscend E5 [14]. Xilinx offers similar products [19]. Devices consisting solely of reconfigurable logic are common in the embedded systems world. The most widely used form of large-scale single device reconfigurable logic is the Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). Even on most hybrid devices, the reconfigurable part is a (limited) FPGA. FPGAs are discussed further, as part of our case study in section 6.

div.head: Process Model
div.p: A process set ∆ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } is scheduled by a fixed priority scheme: the highestpriority runnable process executes on the processor at any time. Priorities are unique, ranging from 1(lowest)..n(highest). Each process τ i has a period T i and deadline D i , where D i ≤ T i . For a sporadic process, T i denotes the minimum inter-arrival time between successive executions of it. The worst-case response time of τ i is R i . Whilst executing, processes cannot voluntarily suspend; also (a restriction later removed) they share no resources, hence do not block.

The limited parallel model allows part of a process to be executed in a coprocessor implemented in reconfigurable hardware. As this is not reflected in the traditional state model of a process, we introduce a new state termed waiting. The extended model is shown in Figure 3 with states (labeled by initial: Idle, Ready, Executing, Blocked, Waiting) and allowed transitions. The processor is always assigned to the highest-priority process among those ready, with that process switching to executing state. When control is passed to a hardware co-processor, the respective process transitions from executing to waiting. It switches to ready state when the co-processor function terminates. Note that the scheduler may need to reconsider the process to execute whenever a co-processor function terminates, as the process switching to ready state may be of higher priority than the one executing.

The part of a process implemented by a coprocessor is termed a gap, as it forms an interruption in the conventional processor based execution of a process. A process can invoke a number of hardware co-processor functions during an invocation, hence can contain a number of gaps. The total time of computation for a specific invocation of a process τ i equals the sum of the execution times in software and on the co-processor. Assuming no correlation between the two, C i = X i + G i , where C i , X i , G i are the upper bounds for overall, software and coprocessor execution times. If a process τ i has no gaps, it requires all its execution time on the processor and the amount of outstanding computation is reduced only when it is scheduled. But if G i > 0, the process may require upto X i scheduled on the processor, but may at some point initiate a hardware co-processor operation. Note that a hardware operation initiated by τ i at time t will complete at t+ g (where g is the length of the gap) and is not dependent on any other process. At any time upto n processes could be in the waiting state having invoked hardware co-processor operations.

div.head: Identifing The Worst Case
div.p: A process may interfere with lower priority proceses only while executing on the processor, ie. in the executing state. When it is in waiting state, computation is performed on the coprocessor, with the processor available to other processes that are in ready state. Thus, each instance of τ j can interfere with lower-priority processes for at most X j time units. For an instance of τ i , cumulative interference equals the individual interferences exerted by each τ j ∈hp(i) summed:

Under the conventional master/slave model, worst-case interference on τ i occurs for simultaneous process releases. This is termed the critical instant [11]. For the limited parallel model, this is no more the worst case. Consider the trivial example in Figure 5. If higher-priority processes A, B start with gaps and all releases coincide, the lowest-priority process can execute on the processor during that time interval and terminate, with no interference (Figure 5(a)). But if it is released one time unit later, its response time time increases (Figure 5(b)).

div.head: Response Time Analysis
div.p: For the worst-case given by the previous section, the number of releases of τ j that can interfere with τ i is (R i + G j )/T j . This expression is analogous to the inclusion of jitter in conventional fixed priority timing analysis [3]. Hence:

div.formula: w n+1 i =C i + j∈hp(i) (w n i +G j )/T j * X i
div.p: The recurrence is initiated by w 0 =C i and terminates when w n+1 =w n .

div.head: Priority Assignment
div.p: Under the conventional master/slave model the Deadline Monotonic Priority Ordering (DMPO) is optimal [9]; under the limited parallel model not. For example, the process set described in Table 2 is not feasible under DMPO but under reversed priorities, it is (see Figure 7). For the limited parallel model, priorities can be optimally assigned by the approach described in [2]. Starting with the lowest priority, processes are tested for feasibility at that priority level. If none is feasible then neither is the whole set. But if one is found feasible then it is assigned that priority and the procedure continues with the remaining processes and priority levels. Provided the worst-case response time of a process can not increase if priorities are exchanged with a higher-priority process, this algorithm is valid and optimal; this property holds for the response time analysis of section 3.4.

div.head: Realisation On FPGAs
div.p: Unlike the program once, logic-term PAL / GAL devices, Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FP-GAs) provide reprogrammability and logic functions to the system designer [19,1]. This allows them to provide more complex functionality than an equivalently sized programmable logic device. A typical sea-of-gates FPGA consists of an array of functional blocks, connected by programmable interconnects (see Figure 2 FPGAs can be used for the physical realisation of the limited parallel architectures depicted in Figures 1(b),1(c). An FPGA connected to the processor-memory bus can provide one or more functions. These typically have high cost when implemented in software and can be sped up if implemented in hardware, eg. digital signal/image processing or parallel algorithms. Multiple parallel functions in an FPGA (ie. as Figure 1(c)) require either internally multiplexing a single bus connection or using the many I/O pins for many separate connections.

FPGAs are reprogrammable; configuration takes some milliseconds. The program for the device can be specified in languages such as Ada [16,17,18], Handel-C [5], VHDL. In any case, the program is synthesised to a net list: an abstract circuit description. This is fitted to the device it is to be implemented on. Finally the fitted design is converted to the configuration bit stream used for programming the FPGA.

div.head: An Example System
div.p: In the example system (Figure 9), a Xilinx Spar-tanIIE connected to RAM is programmed with a softcore Z80 processor plus hardware functions for speed-up. The application is a marble chute sorter (see Figure 10). Marbles (from a random collection) released down the chute from a hopper are detected as either metal/glass half way down the chute, a flipper at the bottom controlling which container they end up in. The functionality consists of the following processes: • Hopper: releases marbles down the chute; • Metal: driven on interrupt from metal sensor; • Glass: likewise, from light sensor; • Flipper: controls where marbles end up.

The flipper and hopper releases are offset by the time (0.2s) it takes for marbles to fall from the hopper to past the sensors. The hardware functions implemented are effectively device drivers for the hopper, sensors and flipper. For the sensors, the driver de-bounces sensor inputs and timestamps readings. Hence, the sensor processes begin with the hardware function and end with software execution (ie. f R =true). The hopper and flipper processes have the hardware function somewhere in the middle of their lifecycle. The timing requirements are given in Table 3. Process offsets are omitted, as they are ignored in response time calculation for the limited parallel model. Placing functions in hardware enables tighter response times; note that if execution was all in software, deadlines would be missed due to additional interference.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Under the introduced limited parallel model for real-time systems, software processes can invoke complex hardware functions at any time, the processor being assigned to another runnable process immediately. Again, at most one process can execute on the processor at any time but they can all execute hardware functions in As for open research issues: Firstly, the analysis must incorporate software blocking. While this is straightforward (by adding a blocking term in the response time equation, as in conventional analysis), the priority assignment method then becomes non-optimal. Blocking must also be extended to hardware shared resources. Secondly, moving functions to ware exchanges processor time with FPGA space. An open issue is the consideration of FPGA space constraints together with timing analysis at the design stage, for implementation decisions.
